```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  results = "asis"
)
library(jsonlite)
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")

summary_data <- fromJSON("black_death_and_late_mediaeval_crisis_summary.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
settlements_raw <- fromJSON("black_death_and_late_mediaeval_crisis_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)

total_area_km2 <- as.numeric(summary_data$total_area_km2)
settlement_count <- as.integer(summary_data$settlement_count)
subregions_list <- summary_data$subregions
domain_totals <- summary_data$domain_totals
hgis_units <- summary_data$hgis_featured_units
hgis_regimes <- summary_data$hgis_regime_summary

pop_1347 <- as.numeric(domain_totals[["1347"]])
pop_1400 <- as.numeric(domain_totals[["1400"]])
pop_1450 <- as.numeric(domain_totals[["1450"]])
pop_1500 <- as.numeric(domain_totals[["1500"]])

na_region <- Filter(function(x) identical(as.character(x$id), "bd_north_atlantic"), subregions_list)[[1]]
na_area <- as.numeric(na_region$area_km2)
europe_area_excl_na <- total_area_km2 - na_area

region_name_map <- setNames(
  vapply(subregions_list, function(x) as.character(x$name), character(1)),
  vapply(subregions_list, function(x) as.character(x$id), character(1))
)

fmt_pct_signed <- function (arg0_val, arg1_digits = 1L) {
  v <- as.numeric(arg0_val)
  prefix <- if (v > 0) "+" else ""
  paste0(prefix, viscount_fmt_number(v, arg1_digits), "%")
}

fmt_source_label <- function (arg0_code) {
  lbl <- gsub("_", " ", as.character(arg0_code), fixed = TRUE)
  lbl <- sub("^Buringh European Urban 700 2000$", "Buringh European Urban (700-2000)", lbl)
  lbl <- sub("^HistoGIS HRE Imperial Circles 1512$", "HistoGIS HRE Imperial Circles (1512)", lbl)
  lbl <- sub("^Historical Basemaps 1500$", "Historical Basemaps (1500)", lbl)
  lbl <- sub("^National Statistical Census Faroe Islands$", "National Statistical Census of the Faroe Islands", lbl)
  lbl
}
```

# Abstract

Between 1347AD and 1500AD the population of Europe outside the East European Plain, together with Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland, underwent the sharpest demographic contraction in recorded continental history. Across `r viscount_fmt_number(total_area_km2, 1L)` km² (`r viscount_fmt_number(europe_area_excl_na, 1L)` km² excluding the North Atlantic archipelagos and Greenland), human numbers fell from `r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1347)` on the eve of the Black Death in 1347 to `r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1400)` in 1400, a net loss of 29,98% at an average annual rate of -0,67%. Recurrent outbreaks of *Yersinia pestis*, prolonged warfare in France, Bohemia and the Balkans, climatic cooling and structural agrarian retreat held population depressed through the early fifteenth century before gradual recovery lifted the continental total to `r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1450)` in 1450 and `r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1500)` in 1500, still 9,82% below the 1347 peak. Continental density declined from 11,98 inhabitants per km² in 1347 (17,22 per km² excluding the North Atlantic and Greenland) to 8,39 in 1400 (12,06 excluding the North Atlantic), recovering to 10,81 (15,53 excluding the North Atlantic) by 1500. Mortality and recovery were highly uneven across the 11 ecological and political sub-regions: by 1400 the British Isles had lost 43,5% of their population, Scandinavia and Finland 38%, Italy and Malta 36,3% and France and the Low Countries 36%, whereas Poland and the Baltic Lands contracted by only 10,4% and stood 15,6% above their 1347 level by 1500. Across the southeast, Ottoman conquest over Thrace, Bulgaria, Serbia and Greece reshaped Balkan settlement while turning Istanbul (200k) and Edirne (127k) into Europe's two largest cities by 1500. Reconciling fiscal registers, palaeoecological pollen trajectories, osteological mortality series, 16 historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations at 1500 (40,95M inhabitants across 2.008.829 km²) and a gazetteer of `r formatC(settlement_count, format = "d", big.mark = ".")` settlements across 41 jurisdictions reveals a striking structural paradox: even while total population in 1500 remained nearly a tenth below 1347, recorded urban population rose 34,87% from 6,89M to 9,3M as surviving rural labour consolidated into regional market towns and territorial capitals.

# Background

In the autumn of 1347 Europe was carrying more people than at any earlier point in its history, yet its agrarian economy was already under visible strain. Three centuries of high mediaeval woodland clearance, fen drainage, upland terracing and village foundation had lifted the continental population outside the East European Plain to `r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1347)`. Densities exceeded 41 inhabitants per km² across the Italian Peninsula and Malta, 34 per km² across France and the Low Countries, 29 per km² across the German Empire, Austria and Switzerland and 23,5 per km² across the British Isles. Marginal soils had been pulled under the plough from the Norwegian fjords to the Pennine moors and the Apennine foothills, fragmenting peasant holdings to subsistence minimums [@Broadberry2015; @Campbell2016]. Between 1315 and 1322 a succession of cold, rain-sodden summers triggered the Great Famine across northern Europe and the Great Bovine Pestilence across Britain, Ireland, France and Germany, wiping out draught oxen and halting demographic growth a full generation before plague arrived [@Campbell2016; @Pribyl2020Survey].

The biological shock that broke the high mediaeval demographic ceiling arrived from the Black Sea trade network in the second half of 1347. Ancient DNA recovered from London's East Smithfield emergency cemetery and contemporary European burial grounds confirms that the pathogen was *Yersinia pestis*, carried westwards from central Asian rodent reservoirs via the Golden Horde siege of Genoese Caffa in Crimea [@Rajaraman2013Genome; @Navid2009Genome; @Parker2023Century]. Merchant galleys brought the bacterium to Constantinople in the summer of 1347 and to Messina in October 1347; by the winter of 1347-1348 it had taken hold in Genoa, Venice, Pisa, Marseille, Mallorca and Barcelona [@Benedictow2004]. Over the next five years the epidemic moved inland along river valleys, maritime shipping lanes and grain corridors. It devastated Tuscany, Languedoc, Provence, Castile and southern England in 1348, swept through Paris, the Low Countries, Ireland, Scotland, Norway and the Rhineland in 1349, crossed Denmark, Sweden, Prussia and northern Germany in 1350 and reached peripheral Baltic and East-Central European districts between 1351 and 1353 [@Benedictow2004; @Campbell2016].

Had the Black Death remained a single catastrophic visitation, European populations might have regained their 1347 numbers within two or three generations, as pre-industrial societies normally do when land becomes abundant and real wages climb. Instead, *Yersinia pestis* established enzootic reservoirs inside Europe itself and returned repeatedly throughout the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries [@Parker2023Century; @Campbell2016]. Genomic sequencing of fourteenth-century skeletal remains demonstrates that the *pestis secunda* of 1360-1363 — noted by chroniclers as a mortality of children and young adults born since 1348 — descended directly from the 1347-1353 European clade rather than requiring a fresh central Asian introduction [@Parker2023Century]. Further continental or macro-regional outbreaks struck in 1369, 1374-1375, 1382-1383, 1390, 1400-1404 (finally reaching Iceland in 1402-1404), 1420-1424, 1438-1439 and 1478-1480 [@Galanaud2015Historical; @Galanaud2020Mortality]. As modern mortality-shock analysis confirms, recurrent epidemic hits spaced a decade apart flatten cohort replacement and suppress aggregate growth far longer than a single acute crisis [@Liu2026Long].

Disease interacted with warfare, fiscal extraction and climatic deterioration across every quadrant of the continent. In France, the Hundred Years' War (1337-1453) unleashed English *chevauchées*, mercenary *routiers* and the Armagnac-Burgundian civil war over Picardy, Normandy, Île-de-France, Guyenne and Champagne, turning plague depopulation into prolonged rural desertion. Across the German lands, Austria and northern Europe, low grain prices and scarce tenants drove thousands of marginal villages out of cultivation, creating the classic late mediaeval *Wüstungen* (deserted settlements) and Norwegian *ødegårder*. In Bohemia, relative fourteenth-century resilience gave way to sharp disruption during the Hussite Wars (1419-1434) before stabilising under Poděbrady and Jagiellonian rule. Along the Arctic margin, deteriorating sea-ice conditions, declining walrus-ivory markets and isolation from Bergen extinguished the Norse Western Settlement in Greenland during the mid-fourteenth century and the Eastern Settlement during the fifteenth century [@Dugmore2012].

In southeastern Europe, plague coincided with a thorough geopolitical transformation. The Serbian Empire of Stefan Dušan fractured after 1355 and the Second Bulgarian Empire split into rival tsardoms just as the Ottoman beylik crossed the Dardanelles to seize Gallipoli in 1354. Ottoman forces captured Adrianople (Edirne) in 1362, crushed Serbian armies on the Maritsa in 1371 and at Kosovo Polje in 1389, annexed Bulgaria by 1393-1396, defeated crusading forces at Nicopolis (1396) and Varna (1444), took Constantinople in May 1453 and absorbed Serbia (1459), the Morea (1460) and Bosnia (1463). Warfare initially emptied plains across Thrace and northern Bulgaria, yet Ottoman *timar* land grants, forced urban transfers (*sürgün*) and Turcoman Yörük colonisation subsequently repopulated Rumelian valleys and lifted Istanbul and Edirne to demographic primacy across all of Europe by 1500 [@Buringh2021].

# Methodology

Reconstructing European population between 1347AD and 1500AD marks a decisive methodological shift from earlier prehistoric and high mediaeval chapters. For the first time across much of Western, Southern and Southeastern Europe, territorial states and city-republics generated nominative fiscal surveys, hearth counts, manorial court rolls, urban tax cadastres and cadastral *tahrir* registers capable of anchoring absolute population levels independently of purely ecological estimates [@Russell1958; @Broadberry2015; @Malanima1998]. Because those documentary registers remain unevenly distributed across time and space — dense in England, Tuscany, Burgundy and parts of the Low Countries, sparser in Scandinavia, Ireland and the Carpathians — MAGNETIC triangulates fiscal headcounts against palaeoecological cereal-pollen curves, osteological mortality series, urban settlement trajectories and 1500 historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations.

## Sub-Regional Partition and Benchmark Architecture

The study domain encompasses `r viscount_fmt_number(total_area_km2, 1L)` km² partitioned into 11 geographically and historically coherent sub-regions. Excluding Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland (`r viscount_fmt_number(na_area, 1L)` km², dominated by the uninhabited Greenland ice cap), mainland and insular Europe spans `r viscount_fmt_number(europe_area_excl_na, 1L)` km². The 11 units capture both shared epidemiological corridors and distinct political trajectories: British Isles; France & Low Countries; German Empire, Austria & Switzerland; Italian Peninsula & Malta; Iberian Kingdoms & Atlantic Islands; Scandinavia & Finland; Iceland, Faroe Islands & Greenland; Poland & Baltic Lands; Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia & Hungary; Wallachia, Moldavia & Transylvania; and Balkans & Ottoman Rumelia.

Four chronological benchmarks — 1347, 1400, 1450 and 1500 — structure the macro-regional trajectories. Setting the opening horizon at 1347 captures Europe immediately before the autumn landfall of *Yersinia pestis* in Sicily, preserving direct continuity with the high mediaeval peak. The 1400 benchmark captures the cumulative demographic trough produced by the 1347-1353 pandemic plus three to four subsequent fourteenth-century recurrences (*pestis secunda* and *pestis tertia*). The 1450 benchmark tests mid-fifteenth-century stagnation and nascent recovery across western and central zones while registering the ongoing North Atlantic decline and the eve of the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople. The terminal 1500 benchmark links directly to early modern territorial censuses and historical GIS administrative polygons.

## Fiscal Registers, Hearth Counts and Manorial Series

Primary fiscal records anchor sub-regional totals wherever surviving archives permit direct enumeration. In England, the Poll Tax of 1377 levied four pence on every lay person aged 14 and over across 37 counties, yielding 1,355M recorded taxpayers; after correcting for under-14 cohorts (roughly 35% of the population), ecclesiastical personnel, exempt paupers and modest evasion, demographic historians derive an English population near 2,5M to 2,8M in 1377, down sharply from roughly 4,75M to 5,5M in 1347 [@Broadberry2015; @Russell1958]. Manorial tithing lists from Essex, Somerset and Gloucestershire, combined with Welsh, Scottish and Irish estimates adjusted for lower pre-plague densities, fix the British Isles trajectory from 7,35M in 1347 to 4,15M in 1400 and 4,95M in 1500 [@Broadberry2015; @Campbell2016].

In Italy, the Florentine *Catasto* of 1427 stands as the most detailed fiscal census of the European Middle Ages, enumerating 60.000 households (264k individuals) across Florence, Pisa, Pistoia, Arezzo, Volterra, Cortona and their rural *contadi* with exact ages, household structures and property holdings [@Malanima1998]. Complemented by merchant correspondence networks such as the Datini archive of Prato [@Deglinnocenti2025Narration], Venetian and Milanese fiscal estimates and southern Italian hearth counts (*fuochi*), the *Catasto* documents an urban and rural drop of roughly 35% to 45% across north-central Italy between 1347 and 1427, grounding the peninsula's trajectory from 12,4M in 1347 to 7,9M in 1400 and 10,6M in 1500 [@Malanima1998].

In France and Burgundy, hearth taxes (*fouages*) and municipal tax rolls provide longitudinal visibility across recurrent plague waves. Spatial analysis of Dijon's municipal tax registers across 1375-1400 demonstrates both sharp intra-urban mortality clustering and rapid post-epidemic replacement via immigration from surrounding villages [@Galanaud2015Historical; @Galanaud2020Mortality]. Combined with the 1328 *État des paroisses et des feux* baseline and late fifteenth-century French royal fiscal reconstructions, hearth series establish the France & Low Countries decline from 20,95M in 1347 to 13,4M in 1400 and partial rebound to 17,65M in 1500. In Poland, where hearth registers begin later, peasant village court records (*księgi sądowe wiejskie*) and credit transactions corroborate steady agrarian continuity and rapid fifteenth-century expansion [@Guzowski2013]. In Ottoman Rumelia, fifteenth-century cadastral tax surveys (*tahrir defterleri*) and poll-tax (*cizye*) rolls document household totals across Thrace, Macedonia, Bulgaria and Serbia, revealing both the initial depopulation of frontier plains and the rapid urban build-up of Edirne and Istanbul.

## Palaeoecological Land-Use Proxies and Bioarchaeology

Documentary sources alone suffer from a well-known spatial bias: regions with dense manorial and urban bureaucracies (England, Tuscany, Provence, Flanders) leave copious mortality records, whereas rural East-Central Europe, parts of Iberia and the northern Balkans leave far fewer fiscal rolls. To test whether documentary silence in Poland, Bohemia and the Carpathians reflected lower mortality or merely missing archives, MAGNETIC incorporates the continental palaeoecological synthesis of Izdebski and colleagues [@Izdebski2022]. Analysing 1.634 pollen samples from 261 radiocarbon-dated sediment cores across 19 European regions, that study tracks changes in cereal cultivation (*Cerealia*-type pollen) between 1250 and 1450. Regions hit hardest by documentary accounts — central Italy, southern France, Greece, southern Sweden and Norway — exhibit abrupt drops in cereal pollen and rapid forest regrowth after 1350, whereas Poland, Bohemia and parts of Ireland and inland Iberia show stable or rising cereal cultivation [@Izdebski2022].

Bioarchaeological series provide an independent check on selective mortality and demographic resilience. Analysis of London skeletal assemblages predating and postdating 1348 demonstrates that although the initial Black Death killed across all age classes, it disproportionately removed frail individuals; survivors and their immediate descendants in the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries experienced measurable improvements in age-specific survival and stature linked to higher real wages and improved nutrition [@Dewitte2014Mortality].

## Urban Gazetteer Integration and 1500 Historical GIS Anchors

Sub-regional aggregates are paired with a georeferenced settlement register of `r formatC(settlement_count, format = "d", big.mark = ".")` localities active between 1347 and 1500 across 41 modern jurisdictions. Primary urban series from Eltjo Buringh's European Urban database (1.933 cities, 99,49% of the register) [@Buringh2021], cross-checked against Bairoch, Batou and Chèvre [@Bairoch1988], form the quantitative backbone. To close sparse Arctic coverage in the North Atlantic sub-region, the register integrates two census-anchored Faroese municipalities from the National Statistical Census of the Faroe Islands (Tórshavn and Klaksvík), two mediaeval Icelandic archaeological localities from the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus (Rangárbotnar and Svinavath, active through 1450 alongside Buringh's Reykjavik) and six small Faroese coastal communities from the GeoNames Municipal Gazetteer Supplement (0,31% crowd-sourced share overall).

At the 1500 terminal horizon, sub-regional totals are audited directly against 16 historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations compiled from two institutional spatial regimes: 11 Imperial Circles of the Holy Roman Empire from the HistoGIS Austrian Academy of Sciences corpus (reflecting the 1512 *Reichskreise* framework scaled to 1500, totalling 16,6M inhabitants across 865.211 km²) and 5 early modern territorial kingdom polygons from Historical Basemaps 1500 (France, Poland-Lithuania, England, Portugal and Scotland, totalling 24,35M inhabitants across 1.143.618 km²). Together these 16 polygons cover 40,95M people — 53,01% of the entire 1500 continental population — providing a spatially explicit institutional cross-check at the transition into the early modern era.

# Validation

## Reconciling High-Mortality and Moderate-Mortality Historiography

Few debates in European historical demography have been more intense than the scale of Black Death mortality between 1347 and 1353. Early twentieth-century syntheses anchored by Josiah Cox Russell placed initial pandemic losses near 20% to 35% of Europe's population [@Russell1958]. Half a century later, Ole Benedictow assembled local tax, manorial and clerical-benefice mortality series from Italy, Spain, France, England and Norway to argue for an average pandemic death toll approaching 60% [@Benedictow2004]. Subsequent work by Broadberry, Campbell and colleagues on English manorial and fiscal accounts revised English mortality during 1348-1350 to roughly 45% to 50%, followed by further net decline to 1400 [@Broadberry2015; @Campbell2016], while the palaeoecological pollen synthesis of Izdebski and colleagues demonstrated that projecting western European mortality uniformly onto Poland, Bohemia or inland Iberia overstates the continental aggregate [@Izdebski2022].

The MAGNETIC trajectory reconciles these positions without adopting either extreme as a continental universal. Across the 11 sub-regions combined, population declines by 29,98% between 1347 (`r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1347)`) and 1400 (`r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1400)`). That continental average conceals a fourfold regional spread: the British Isles drop by 43,5% (7,35M to 4,15M), closely tracking manorial and 1377 Poll Tax benchmarks [@Broadberry2015]; Scandinavia and Finland fall by 38% (2,45M to 1,52M), matching severe Norwegian farm desertion; Italy and Malta decline by 36,3% (12,4M to 7,9M), consistent with the 1427 *Catasto* and Tuscan and Lombard urban rolls [@Malanima1998]; and France and the Low Countries contract by 36% (20,95M to 13,4M), reflecting combined plague and Hundred Years' War losses [@Galanaud2020Mortality]. Conversely, Poland and the Baltic Lands fall by just 10,4% (4,63M to 4,15M), while Bohemia-Hungary and Wallachia-Moldavia-Transylvania each decline by 13,3%, aligning with cereal-pollen continuity and village court activity [@Izdebski2022; @Guzowski2013]. In short, the 45% to 55% mortality model fits the densely commercialised maritime and urban core of Western Europe and Norway, whereas the continental average sits closer to 30% once lightly struck East-Central European lowlands and partial inter-wave rebounds between 1353 and 1400 are weighed in proportion to population.

## Cross-Checking Against 1500 Historical GIS Sub-Administrative Enumerations

Auditing the terminal 1500 benchmark against the 16 historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations confirms internal coherence across Western, Central and East-Central Europe while clarifying jurisdictional boundary differences (Table 1).

```{r table_hgis_1500}
hgis_rows <- lapply(hgis_units, function(u) {
  pop_v <- as.numeric(u$population)
  area_v <- as.numeric(u$area_km2)
  dens_v <- pop_v / area_v
  reg_tag <- if (identical(as.character(u$country), "HRE")) "Holy Roman Empire" else "Early Modern Kingdom"
  data.frame(
    Unit = as.character(u$unit_name),
    Jurisdiction = reg_tag,
    Source = fmt_source_label(u$source),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(area_v, 0L),
    Pop1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(pop_v),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens_v, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
hgis_df <- do.call(rbind, hgis_rows)

tot_hre <- hgis_regimes[[1]]
tot_bm <- hgis_regimes[[2]]
sum_area <- as.numeric(tot_hre$area_km2_sum) + as.numeric(tot_bm$area_km2_sum)
sum_pop <- as.numeric(tot_hre$population_sum) + as.numeric(tot_bm$population_sum)

hgis_summary_rows <- data.frame(
  Unit = c("Subtotal: HRE Imperial Circles (11 units)", "Subtotal: Kingdom Basemaps (5 units)", "Combined 1500 HGIS Enumeration (16 units)"),
  Jurisdiction = c("Holy Roman Empire", "Kingdom Polygons", "All 1500 HGIS Units"),
  Source = c("HistoGIS HRE Imperial Circles (1512)", "Historical Basemaps (1500)", "Two institutional regimes"),
  Area = c(
    viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(tot_hre$area_km2_sum), 0L),
    viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(tot_bm$area_km2_sum), 0L),
    viscount_fmt_number(sum_area, 0L)
  ),
  Pop1500 = c(
    viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tot_hre$population_sum)),
    viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(tot_bm$population_sum)),
    viscount_fmt_pop(sum_pop)
  ),
  Density = c(
    viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(tot_hre$population_sum) / as.numeric(tot_hre$area_km2_sum), 2L),
    viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(tot_bm$population_sum) / as.numeric(tot_bm$area_km2_sum), 2L),
    viscount_fmt_number(sum_pop / sum_area, 2L)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
hgis_full_df <- rbind(hgis_df, hgis_summary_rows)
rownames(hgis_full_df) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  hgis_full_df,
  caption = "Historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations at the 1500 horizon across 16 Holy Roman Empire and early modern kingdom polygons.",
  col_names = c("Administrative Unit", "Polity Class", "Source Corpus", "Area (km²)", "1500 Pop.", "Density (per km²)")
)
```

Three direct cross-checks emerge from Table 1. First, the 11 Imperial Circles of the Holy Roman Empire sum to 16,6M across 865.211 km² (mean density 19,19 inhabitants per km²). Once Burgundischer Kreis (2,1M, largely belonging to the Low Countries) and the Bohemian-Moravian core inside Kreisfreies Gebiet (2,6M covering Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia and Switzerland) are reallocated to their respective sub-regions, the remaining German and Austrian Imperial Circles align cleanly with the 13,5M benchmark assigned to German Empire, Austria & Switzerland (28,06 per km² across 481.097,9 km²), capturing the high density of Schwäbischer Kreis (43,73 per km²) and Fränkischer Kreis (31,6 per km²) against sparser northern plains in Niedersächsischer Kreis (17,93 per km²) and Obersächsischer Kreis (18,04 per km²).

Second, early modern kingdom polygons in Historical Basemaps 1500 place France at 15,5M across 429.261 km² (36,11 per km²); adding the Low Countries (roughly 2,15M, consistent with Burgundischer Kreis at 2,1M) reproduces the 17,65M total for France & Low Countries within 0,5%. Similarly, England (2,6M) plus Scotland (550k) give 3,15M for Great Britain excluding Wales, leaving 1,8M across Wales and Ireland inside the 4,95M British Isles total — a ratio consistent with English fiscal primacy [@Broadberry2015]. Third, Portugal (1,2M at 12,94 per km²) sits proportionally inside the 8,95M Iberian total alongside Castile, Aragon, Navarre and Granada, while Poland-Lithuania (4,5M within its western 1500 polygon of 339.334 km², density 13,26 per km²) aligns directly with the 5,35M Poland & Baltic Lands sub-region once Prussian, Pomeranian and Livonian territories are included [@Guzowski2013].

## Bioarchaeological Survival, Urban Migration and Pollen Cross-Checks

Independent micro-demographic studies further corroborate the macro-regional rebound profile between 1400 and 1500. In Dijon, where municipal tax rolls survive across three successive plagues between 1375 and 1400, household counts recovered far faster than natural birth-minus-death surpluses could allow because landless migrants and younger rural cohorts poured into vacant urban workshops [@Galanaud2015Historical; @Galanaud2020Mortality]. That mechanism explains why the 1.943-settlement urban register expanded from 6,27M in 1400 to 9,3M in 1500 (+48,17%) while continental total population rose by only 28,81%. At the same time, London skeletal survival curves confirm improved post-plague adult longevity [@Dewitte2014Mortality], while English summer-drought reconstructions remind us that harvest volatility persisted into the fifteenth century and periodically checked rural recovery [@Pribyl2020Survey].

# Results

## Continental Trajectory and Sub-Regional Divergence

Across the full 153-year span from 1347AD to 1500AD, Europe's population followed a deep asymmetric V-shaped trough (Figure 1 and Table 2). Total population fell by 25,69M between 1347 and 1400 (`r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1347)` to `r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1400)`), a loss of 29,98%. Recovery remained sluggish during the first half of the fifteenth century, adding 6,06M (+10,1%) by 1450 (`r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1450)`), before accelerating across the second half of the century to add 11,22M (+17%) by 1500 (`r viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1500)`). Even at 1500, Europe outside the East European Plain still carried 8,41M fewer people (-9,82%) than on the eve of the pandemic.

```{r fig_pop_trajectory}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/black_death_and_late_mediaeval_crisis_population_trajectory.png",
  caption = "Sub-regional and continental population trajectories across 11 European and North Atlantic sub-regions, 1347-1500.",
  label = "fig:pop_trajectory"
)
```

```{r table_subregional_trajectory}
traj_rows <- lapply(subregions_list, function(sr) {
  a <- as.numeric(sr$area_km2)
  p47 <- as.numeric(sr$population[["1347"]])
  p00 <- as.numeric(sr$population[["1400"]])
  p50 <- as.numeric(sr$population[["1450"]])
  p500 <- as.numeric(sr$population[["1500"]])
  chg_1400 <- 100 * (p00 - p47) / p47
  chg_1500 <- 100 * (p500 - p47) / p47
  data.frame(
    Subregion = as.character(sr$name),
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L),
    P1347 = viscount_fmt_pop(p47),
    P1400 = viscount_fmt_pop(p00),
    P1450 = viscount_fmt_pop(p50),
    P1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(p500),
    Chg1400 = fmt_pct_signed(chg_1400, 1L),
    Chg1500 = fmt_pct_signed(chg_1500, 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
traj_df <- do.call(rbind, traj_rows)
tot_row <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Total Study Domain (11 sub-regions)",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(total_area_km2, 0L),
  P1347 = viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1347),
  P1400 = viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1400),
  P1450 = viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1450),
  P1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(pop_1500),
  Chg1400 = fmt_pct_signed(100 * (pop_1400 - pop_1347) / pop_1347, 1L),
  Chg1500 = fmt_pct_signed(100 * (pop_1500 - pop_1347) / pop_1347, 1L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
traj_df <- rbind(traj_df, tot_row)
rownames(traj_df) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  traj_df,
  caption = "Sub-regional population trajectories and percentage changes across Europe and the North Atlantic, 1347-1500.",
  col_names = c("Sub-Region", "Area (km²)", "1347", "1400", "1450", "1500", "1347-1400", "1347-1500")
)
```

The geographic contrast in Table 2 is stark. Every sub-region west of the Elbe-Adriatic axis plus Scandinavia suffered losses between 24% and 43,5% by 1400 and still stood below its 1347 ceiling in 1500. Every sub-region along the East-Central European crescent — Poland and the Baltic Lands, Bohemia-Hungary and Wallachia-Moldavia-Transylvania — suffered modest 10% to 14% contractions by 1400 and exceeded its pre-plague population by 1500. Consequently, Europe's demographic weight shifted measurably eastwards: the three East-Central European sub-regions raised their combined share of the domain from 13,75% in 1347 (11,78M) to 16,5% in 1500 (12,75M), while the British Isles fell from 8,58% to 6,41% and France and the Low Countries declined from 24,46% to 22,85%.

## Western Europe: Poll Tax England, War-Torn France and the Tuscan Catasto

No large European region suffered a deeper or longer demographic depression than the British Isles. From 7,35M in 1347 (23,57 inhabitants per km²), the population of Britain and Ireland plunged to 4,15M in 1400 (-43,5%, 13,31 per km²), edged up only to 4,35M in 1450 and reached 4,95M in 1500 (15,87 per km², still -32,7% below 1347). England's initial plague wave of 1348-1349 killed almost half the rural peasantry and clergy; *pestis secunda* in 1361-1362 struck heavily at children and adolescents, preventing a rapid rebound [@Broadberry2015; @Parker2023Century]. By the 1377 Poll Tax, arable demesnes had been widely leased out, real wages had nearly doubled and landowners across the Midlands were converting abandoned clayland grain parishes into sheep pasture to feed the expanding English woollen-cloth export trade. London contracted from 56,9k in 1347 to 45k in 1400 and stood at 50k in 1500, remaining modest compared to Italian and Ottoman metropolises even as its share of English urban life increased [@Buringh2021].

France and the Low Countries experienced a comparable twin catastrophe of epidemic mortality and military devastation. Population fell from 20,95M in 1347 (34,06 per km²) to 13,4M in 1400 (-36%, 21,79 per km²), recovered slowly to 14,6M in 1450 during the final campaigns of the Hundred Years' War and then surged by more than 3M once peace returned after 1453 to reach 17,65M in 1500 (28,69 per km², -15,8% vs 1347). Urban trajectories inside the sub-region diverged sharply: Paris fell from 64,3k in 1347 to 54k in 1400 before surging to 94k by 1500 as royal administration consolidated, while Bordeaux rose from 30k to 50k and Rouen climbed from 29,9k to 40k. By contrast, the old Flemish cloth capitals faced structural industrial decline alongside plague losses: Gent slid from 64k in 1347-1400 to 45k in 1500 and Brugge slipped from 38,6k to 35k as maritime commerce shifted towards Antwerp and the Dutch estuaries [@Buringh2021; @Bairoch1988].

On the Italian Peninsula and Malta, the densest agrarian and urban landscape in mediaeval Europe bore the earliest and heaviest Mediterranean blow. Population contracted from 12,4M in 1347 (41,28 per km²) to 7,9M in 1400 (-36,3%, 26,3 per km²), rose to 8,8M in 1450 and recovered strongly to 10,6M in 1500 (35,29 per km², -14,5% vs 1347) [@Malanima1998]. Nowhere is the contrast between rural contraction and urban resilience clearer than in Italy. Whereas the Tuscan *Catasto* of 1427 revealed stagnant Florentine numbers (55k throughout 1400-1500 compared to 60,1k in 1347 and far higher pre-1340 estimates), territorial capitals expanded vigorously during the fifteenth century: Napoli more than doubled from 52,4k in 1347 (45k in 1400) to 125k in 1500 under Aragonese rule; Venezia recovered from 55k in 1400 to 100k in 1500; Milano held near 90k to 100k; Roma climbed from 31,4k to 55k after the papal return from Avignon; Palermo grew from 27k in 1400 to 55k in 1500; and Lombard-Venetian industrial cities such as Brescia (25,4k to 49k), Cremona (13,4k to 40k) and Verona (25,9k to 39k) expanded rapidly [@Malanima1998; @Buringh2021].

Iberian Kingdoms and Atlantic Islands suffered a milder aggregate contraction (-24%, from 9,15M in 1347 to 6,95M in 1400) and came within 2,2% of pre-plague totals by 1500 (8,95M, 15,05 per km²). Coastal Catalonia was severely wounded: Barcelona fell steadily from 43k in 1347 to 38k in 1400 and 20k in 1500 amid repeated plagues and civil war. Andalusia also contracted as Sevilla slid from 80k to 45k, Cordoba from 49,6k to 35k and Nasrid Granada from 41,1k to 23k by the decade following its 1492 conquest. Yet Castile's interior plateau expanded sheep transhumance under the *Mesta*, Portugal's maritime boom lifted Lisboa from 43,3k in 1347 to 65k in 1500 and the Crown of Aragon's commercial centre of gravity migrated south to Valencia, which more than doubled from 32,5k in 1347 to 75k in 1500 [@Buringh2021].

## Central Europe, Deserted Villages and East-Central Resilience

Across the German Empire, Austria and Switzerland, population fell by 29,7% from 13,95M in 1347 (29 per km²) to 9,8M in 1400 (20,37 per km²), then posted the strongest fifteenth-century percentage rebound in Europe (+37,8% from 1400 to 1500) to reach 13,5M (28,06 per km², just -3,2% below 1347). That rebound did not simply restore the pre-plague settlement grid. Throughout Swabia, Franconia, Hesse, Thuringia, Lower Saxony and Brandenburg, between 20% and 35% of high mediaeval villages became permanent *Wüstungen* during the late fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries as surviving peasants vacated upland clearings and poor sandy soils for fertile river valleys and chartered towns. Fifteenth-century growth therefore concentrated in larger nucleated villages, Alpine mining districts (Tyrol and Saxony) and imperial commercial cities led by Koeln (45k in 1500), Nürnberg, Augsburg, Lübeck and Wien.

East of the Oder and Morava, the demographic trajectory diverged markedly from Western Europe. Poland and the Baltic Lands declined by only 10,4% between 1347 (4,63M, 9,72 per km²) and 1400 (4,15M, 8,71 per km²), had already surpassed their pre-plague total by 1450 (4,65M) and reached 5,35M in 1500 (+15,6% above 1347, 11,23 per km²). Both archival village court series and regional cereal-pollen curves confirm that lower settlement density, sparser maritime connectivity away from the Baltic ports and active royal colonisation under Casimir the Great cushioned inland Poland against catastrophic rural collapse [@Izdebski2022; @Guzowski2013]. Rising Western European demand for Baltic rye and timber simultaneously propelled Gdansk to 30k inhabitants by 1500 and doubled recorded urban totals across the sub-region from 153k in 1347 to 310k in 1500.

Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia and Hungary followed a similar low-mortality path between 1347 (4,9M, 22,42 per km²) and 1400 (4,25M, -13,3%), when Imperial capital patronage lifted Praha from 19,2k in 1347 to 40k in 1400. Subsequent growth slowed to 4,45M in 1450 as the Hussite Wars devastated Bohemian towns and rural estates, reducing Praha to 30k by 1500, yet Hungarian and Slovak agrarian expansion carried the sub-region to 4,95M in 1500 (+1% above 1347, 22,65 per km²). Adjacent Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania likewise lost 13,3% by 1400 (2,25M to 1,95M) before expanding to 2,15M in 1450 and 2,45M in 1500 (+8,9% above 1347, 9,36 per km²), anchored by Transylvanian Saxon towns and Moldavian commercial hubs such as Suceava (10k).

## Nordic Contraction and the Extinction of Norse Greenland

Northern Europe experienced the longest agrarian retreat outside the British Isles. In Scandinavia and Finland, population dropped by 38% from 2,45M in 1347 (2,11 per km²) to 1,52M in 1400 (1,31 per km²), recovering modestly to 1,68M in 1450 and 1,85M in 1500 (1,59 per km², still -24,5% below 1347). Norway suffered the deepest rural collapse: after *Yersinia pestis* landed at Bergen in 1349, upwards of half of all upland and fjord farms were deserted (*ødegårder*), depressing royal tax revenues for two centuries and allowing Hanseatic merchants to dominate Bergen (7k in 1500, the largest town in the Nordic sub-region). Pollen records from southern Sweden and Norway confirm prolonged woodland regeneration across abandoned arable fields [@Izdebski2022], whereas eastern Finland's pioneer *kaski* slash-and-burn frontier continued slow interior expansion.

Across the North Atlantic sub-region — Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland — population fell from 84,7k in 1347 to 59k in 1400 (-30,3%), declined further to 54k in 1450 and stood at 56,7k in 1500 (-33,1% below 1347), making it the only European sub-region with fewer inhabitants in 1500 than in 1400. Two separate shocks produced this trajectory. First, Iceland escaped the 1347-1353 wave entirely only to suffer a devastating plague introduction in 1402-1404 that killed roughly a third to half of its population, followed by a second severe epidemic in 1494-1495. Second, Norse Greenland collapsed altogether: the Western Settlement in Nuuk fjord was abandoned around 1350, and the Eastern Settlement in southern Greenland — last securely documented at the Hvalsey church wedding of 1408 — disappeared during the mid-fifteenth century under compounding pressures of Little Ice Age sea-ice expansion, soil erosion, declining European ivory demand and shrinking shipping links with plague-weakened Norway [@Dugmore2012].

## Ottoman Conquest and Urban Restructuring across the Balkans

In the Balkans and Ottoman Rumelia, population contracted by 22,5% from 7,55M in 1347 (13,78 per km²) to 5,85M in 1400 (10,68 per km²), recovering to 6,25M in 1450 and 6,95M in 1500 (12,69 per km², -7,9% below 1347). Both epidemic mortality and continuous warfare shaped the fourteenth-century trough. Plague struck Constantinople, Thrace and Greece immediately in 1347-1348, followed by cereal-pollen declines across Greek valleys [@Izdebski2022], while Byzantine civil wars and Ottoman campaigns over Thrace, Macedonia, Bulgaria and Serbia depopulated lowland plains and drove Christian peasantry into upland refuge zones across the Pindus, Rhodope and Dinaric ranges.

During the fifteenth century, Ottoman state consolidation inverted the region's urban geography. Immediately before 1453, Byzantine Constantinople had shrunk to a fragmented cluster of quarters inside the Theodosian walls, yet Sultan Mehmed II immediately launched state-directed repopulation (*sürgün*), transferring artisans, merchants and peasants from Anatolia, Thrace, Serbia and Greece into the new imperial capital. In the urban gazetteer, Istanbul climbs from 90k in 1347 and 80k in 1400 to 126,5k at the mid-century benchmark and 200k in 1500, overtaking every city in Latin Christendom [@Buringh2021]. Equally dramatic was the rise of Edirne (Adrianople), the Ottoman Rumelian capital from the 1360s until 1453 and an imperial garrison and commercial hub thereafter: Edirne expanded twentyfold from 6,4k in 1347 to 15k in 1400, 43,6k in 1450 and 127k in 1500, standing second only to Istanbul in all of Europe. By contrast, Saloniki contracted from 46,1k in 1347 to 42k in 1400 and 19k in 1500 after prolonged Venetian-Ottoman sieges, standing just on the threshold of its sixteenth-century revival fuelled by Sephardic Jewish refugees expelled from Spain after 1492.

## Late Mediaeval Urbanisation and the Rank-Size Hierarchy

Comparing the 1.943-settlement urban gazetteer against the 11 macro-regional totals exposes one of the defining structural transformations of late mediaeval Europe (Figure 2 and Table 3). Between 1347 and 1400, recorded urban population dropped by only 8,98% (from 6,89M across 1.802 active settlements to 6,27M across 1.854 settlements), far less than the 29,98% decline in total population. As a result, Europe's recorded urban share climbed immediately from 8,05% in 1347 to 10,46% in 1400. By 1450 urban population had already surpassed its 1347 total (7,35M, 11,13% urban share), and by 1500 it reached 9,3M across 1.941 active settlements — 34,87% higher than in 1347 and representing 12,03% of the entire continental population [@Buringh2021]. The number of cities exceeding 10k inhabitants rose from 109 in both 1347 and 1400 to 121 in 1450 and 195 in 1500, while cities of 50k or more expanded from 10 in 1347 and 9 in 1400 to 15 in 1500.

```{r fig_urban_hierarchy}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/black_death_and_late_mediaeval_crisis_urban_hierarchy.png",
  caption = "Leading European cities and urban rank-size hierarchy across 1.943 recorded settlements, 1347-1500.",
  label = "fig:urban_hierarchy"
)
```

```{r table_top_cities}
top_list <- summary_data$top_settlements
n_top <- min(15L, length(top_list))
city_rows <- lapply(seq_len(n_top), function(i) {
  s <- top_list[[i]]
  rid <- as.character(s$region_id)
  rname <- if (rid %in% names(region_name_map)) region_name_map[[rid]] else rid
  p47 <- as.numeric(s$population[["1347"]])
  p00 <- as.numeric(s$population[["1400"]])
  p500 <- as.numeric(s$population[["1500"]])
  chg <- 100 * (p500 - p47) / p47
  data.frame(
    Rank = as.character(i),
    City = as.character(s$name),
    Jurisdiction = as.character(s$country),
    Subregion = rname,
    P1347 = viscount_fmt_pop(p47),
    P1400 = viscount_fmt_pop(p00),
    P1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(p500),
    Change = fmt_pct_signed(chg, 1L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
city_df <- do.call(rbind, city_rows)
rownames(city_df) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  city_df,
  caption = "Top 15 European cities ranked by peak population between 1347AD and 1500AD.",
  col_names = c("Rank", "City", "Jurisdiction", "Sub-Region", "1347", "1400", "1500", "1347-1500")
)
```

Table 3 captures the redistribution of Europe's urban apex. In 1347 Milano (95,2k), Istanbul (90k), Sevilla (80k), Venezia (71,4k), Genova (69,3k), Paris (64,3k) and Gent (64k) led the continent. By 1500 five cities stood at or above 100k — Istanbul (200k), Edirne (127k), Napoli (125k), Milano (100k) and Venezia (100k) — followed closely by Paris (94k), Valencia (75k) and Lisboa (65k). Three mechanisms drove rising late mediaeval urbanisation despite smaller rural totals: higher post-plague real wages shifted household demand from bare grain toward urban textiles, metalwork and wine; territorial monarchs and Italian signori concentrated fiscal and court expenditure in regional capitals; and continuous rural-to-urban immigration replenished urban workshops after each epidemic shock [@Galanaud2020Mortality; @Malanima1998]. By 1500, recorded urban shares reached 22,4% in Italy and Malta, 18,3% in Iberia and 12,5% in France and the Low Countries, against 4,3% in Scandinavia and Finland and 4,8% in Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania.

# Limitations

Four structural uncertainties govern late mediaeval demographic reconstructions between 1347AD and 1500AD. First, hearth-to-person multipliers are not stationary across epidemic shocks. Pre-plague rural hearths commonly averaged 4,5 to 5 persons, whereas the 1427 Tuscan *Catasto* and post-plague Burgundian tax rolls show mean household sizes compressed to 3,8 to 4,4 persons due to elevated widowhood, orphaned nuclear units and disrupted marriage cohorts [@Malanima1998; @Galanaud2020Mortality]. Applying a rigid multiplier across 1347 and 1400 risks understating the real drop in individuals by 5% to 10%.

Second, the four-benchmark cadence (1347, 1400, 1450, 1500) inevitably smooths violent short-term epidemic oscillations. In reality, many Western European populations dropped more deeply by 1351 than their 1400 total suggests, rebounded modestly in the 1350s, plunged again during *pestis secunda* (1361-1363) and hit an absolute late mediaeval floor anywhere between 1380 and 1440 depending on local warfare and harvest failures [@Campbell2016; @Broadberry2015]. Similarly, linear or exponential interpolation across Ottoman Istanbul's 1450 benchmark smooths the abrupt post-1453 repopulation jump under Mehmed II.

Third, the 1.943-settlement gazetteer inherits the urban threshold of its primary archive [@Buringh2021]. Towns below 1.000 inhabitants and rural *Wüstungen* are largely absent, which concentrates recorded settlements in Italy (387), France and the Low Countries (438) and Iberia (306) while leaving Greenland with zero urban localities and Iceland with two radiocarbon anchors (Rangárbotnar and Svinavath) terminating at 1450. Fourth, the 16 historical GIS enumerations at 1500 reflect dynastic and fiscal boundaries (Burgundischer Kreis, Kreisfreies Gebiet, Poland-Lithuania) that cut across the fixed agro-ecological sub-regional polygons, requiring careful territorial reconciliation when comparing polygon sums against sub-regional totals.

# Conclusion

Between 1347AD and 1500AD Europe absorbed a demographic shock without parallel in the previous millennium and emerged with a markedly different population map. Continental numbers fell by nearly 30% between 1347 (85,66M) and 1400 (59,98M), hovered near 66,03M at mid-century and recovered to 77,26M by 1500 — still almost a tenth shy of pre-plague levels. Mortality and recovery split the continent along clear geographic lines. The densely settled, commercially integrated economies of the British Isles (-43,5% by 1400), Scandinavia (-38%), Italy (-36,3%) and France and the Low Countries (-36%) suffered protracted agrarian contraction, widespread village desertion and a century-long delay in regaining high mediaeval population densities, while Norse Greenland disappeared altogether. By contrast, Poland and the Baltic Lands (-10,4%), Bohemia-Hungary (-13,3%) and Wallachia-Moldavia-Transylvania (-13,3%) experienced far lighter initial losses and stood above their 1347 totals by 1500.

Simultaneously, late mediaeval crisis accelerated two structural shifts that defined early modern Europe. In the southeast, Ottoman conquest over Thrace, Bulgaria, Serbia and Greece consolidated a new imperial core around Istanbul (200k) and Edirne (127k), making Ottoman Rumelia home to Europe's two largest cities in 1500. Across the continent as a whole, scarcer labour, higher real wages, state centralisation and rural-to-urban migration lifted total recorded urban population by 34,87% (6,89M to 9,3M) and raised the continental urban share from 8,05% to 12,03%. When sustained rural fertility and lower epidemic frequency returned after 1500, Europe entered the sixteenth century with a leaner, more urbanised and spatially rebalanced demographic base.

# Appendix

Table 4 summarises recorded settlement coverage, total urban population, urban share of sub-regional population and the leading 1500 city across all 11 sub-regions. Full settlement-level provenance auditing, jurisdictional rankings and top-25 urban trajectories are documented in the companion settlement gazetteer.

```{r table_appendix_urban_summary}
site_reg_vec <- vapply(settlements_raw, function(x) as.character(x$region_id), character(1))
site_name_vec <- vapply(settlements_raw, function(x) as.character(x$name), character(1))
site_p47 <- vapply(settlements_raw, function(x) {
  v <- x$population[["1347"]]
  if (is.null(v)) 0 else as.numeric(v)
}, numeric(1))
site_p500 <- vapply(settlements_raw, function(x) {
  v <- x$population[["1500"]]
  if (is.null(v)) 0 else as.numeric(v)
}, numeric(1))

app_rows <- lapply(subregions_list, function(sr) {
  rid <- as.character(sr$id)
  idx <- which(site_reg_vec == rid)
  n_s <- length(idx)
  u47 <- sum(site_p47[idx])
  u500 <- sum(site_p500[idx])
  p47_tot <- as.numeric(sr$population[["1347"]])
  p500_tot <- as.numeric(sr$population[["1500"]])
  sh47 <- 100 * u47 / p47_tot
  sh500 <- 100 * u500 / p500_tot
  best_i <- idx[which.max(site_p500[idx])]
  lead_str <- paste0(site_name_vec[best_i], " (", viscount_fmt_pop(site_p500[best_i]), ")")
  data.frame(
    Subregion = as.character(sr$name),
    Sites = formatC(n_s, format = "d", big.mark = "."),
    U1347 = viscount_fmt_pop(u47),
    U1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(u500),
    Sh1347 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh47, 1L), "%"),
    Sh1500 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(sh500, 1L), "%"),
    Lead1500 = lead_str,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
app_df <- do.call(rbind, app_rows)
tot_u47 <- sum(site_p47)
tot_u500 <- sum(site_p500)
app_tot <- data.frame(
  Subregion = "Total Study Domain",
  Sites = formatC(settlement_count, format = "d", big.mark = "."),
  U1347 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_u47),
  U1500 = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_u500),
  Sh1347 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * tot_u47 / pop_1347, 1L), "%"),
  Sh1500 = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * tot_u500 / pop_1500, 1L), "%"),
  Lead1500 = "Istanbul (200k)",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
app_df <- rbind(app_df, app_tot)
rownames(app_df) <- NULL
viscount_table(
  app_df,
  caption = "Sub-regional urban settlement totals, urban shares and leading cities across 1.943 localities, 1347-1500.",
  col_names = c("Sub-Region", "Settlements", "1347 Urban", "1500 Urban", "1347 Share", "1500 Share", "Leading City (1500)")
)
```
